title: A hymn in Tilang
hook: Tilang holds Guru Nanak's hymn to Lalo about Babur's invasion, and its promise of a time for truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Tilang, where Guru Nanak's plea leans toward Persian, and your line was persian color. Whose words for the deepest things did you hear? A new week starts. Day one thousand ninety-three.

When is the right time to say a hard, true thing? Right away, while it's raw? Later, when it's safe? Only to the people in charge? A page into the Tilang section, Guru Nanak gives his answer in the middle of a disaster. An army has come down from Kabul. Wedding songs have turned into songs of blood. And the hymn about it is addressed to one man by name, again and again, at the end of its lines: Lalo. Today: a hymn in Tilang, and what it does with the truth.
screen: `WHEN DO YOU SAY THE HARD THING?` → `AN ARMY FROM KABUL.` → `ADDRESSED TO LALO.`

segments.voice: Earlier on this path we heard this shabad as courage, and as a word told first to a working man. Today, watch the moves it makes, one after another. First, it names what went missing. In paraphrase: modesty and dharma have both hidden themselves, and falsehood walks about as the leader. Before the hymn counts any damage, it says what vanished from public life: shame and right living. Second, it names who was pushed aside. The qazis and the brahmins, the religious officials of both communities, have lost their place. Third, it names who suffered, and it doesn't stop at one side. The Muslim women, the hymn says, read their scripture and in their pain cry out to Khuda, God. And women of the Hindu castes, high and low, are counted in the same reckoning. Yesterday we heard Tilang speak in the words of Muslim neighbors. Here, in the same raga, grief crosses the same line. Nobody's suffering is left out to make a point. Fourth, the hymn says when. Near its close, on the next page, Guru Nanak says he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time of truth. That's the answer to the hook's question. Not when it's comfortable. Not only when someone powerful asks. When it's true, and the time has come. That's today's line: truth to power. Notice that the power never gets a vote on the timing. Whatever followed, the shabad was sung, kept, and set in the Granth, where it is still sung in Tilang.
screen: `MODESTY AND DHARMA HAVE HIDDEN.` · `THE QAZIS AND BRAHMINS PUSHED ASIDE.` · `GRIEF ON EVERY SIDE IS COUNTED.` · `TRUTH AT THE TIME OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `TRUTH TO POWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Tilang shabad, or sit with one true sentence. If you can, play a recording of this hymn, often searched as jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee, and just listen. If not, sit quietly and let one true thing come to mind that you haven't said yet. It doesn't have to be about kings or armies. It might be small. Shape it into a single plain sentence in your head, without blame and without softening. Then simply hold it. You don't have to say it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. If you don't, let the sentence rest with your breath. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Tilang. Guru Nanak's song to Lalo about the invasion: what vanished, who was pushed aside, who grieved, and truth told at the time of truth. Today's word.
Your line: truth to power. Today, if a moment comes for your one true sentence, say it plainly, to the person it belongs to, and let it be kind as well as true. Day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Tilang hymn addressed to Bhai Lalo is sung in kirtan in Raga Tilang, and its line about speaking as the Master's word comes is quoted by some Sikhs as a standard for honest speech.

fork.setup: you've seen an invasion up close. the powerful are rising, and you have a song. what do you do with it?
options: keep quiet until things settle down.
sing what you saw, plainly, to a friend by name.
sing it only to the new rulers, carefully.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak sings it to Lalo, naming what vanished, who was pushed aside and who suffered, and says he'll tell the truth at the time of truth.

original.note: lalo, remembered by tradition as a carpenter of Saidpur, the friend this Tilang hymn is addressed to.

trapdoor: what you thought: a protest song against one invader.
what it means: a hymn that names what went missing, who was pushed aside and who grieved on every side, and promises truth at its time.

what a scholar hears: the hymn runs across ang 722–723; it counts both the qazis and brahmins displaced and the women of both communities suffering, and closes with Nanak speaking the word of truth at the time of truth.

sources.ref: Tilang Mahalla 1, Ang 722–723 (jaisee mai aavai khasam kee baanee; modesty and dharma hidden, falsehood leading; qazis and brahmins displaced; Muslim and Hindu women suffering; truth at the time of truth)
Guru Nanak and Bhai Lalo at Saidpur

notes: Paraphrase of the Tilang hymn at Ang 722–723 (saram dharam dui chhap khaloe, koor phirai pardhan; kajian bamana kee gal thakee; musalmaniaa parheh kateba kasat meh kareh khudai; jaat sanaatee hor hidvaaneeaa; sach kee baanee nanak aakhai sach sunaaisee sach kee belaa). Please confirm.

Kept to the text; no date for the invasion and no names beyond Kabul, Lalo and Khuda, which the hymn itself uses (Babur is named in the outline and in the hymn's later lines; not stated in voice to avoid a dated claim).
This hymn was taught at days 40 and 659 and cited at 1014; this day takes a new angle (the hymn's four moves and the grief that crosses communities) to avoid repetition.

Editor pass: cut 'a town is burning' (not in the hymn) for the hymn's own picture of wedding songs turned to songs of blood (khoon ke sohile); dropped the spoken Ang from the hook; softened 'quoted by Sikhs' to 'some Sikhs'; Lalo's trade attributed to tradition.
